card.hook: Picture a long, car-free street with cafe tables, palms and a steady parade of strollers, all lined up like they're waiting for your photo. This was mangrove forest until 1912, which is hard to believe now.
card.stand_here: Head to Pennsylvania Avenue and stand about 210 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The whole length of the mall opens up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the street as you see it. Switch to 0.5x to fit the full width of the mall with the tables and palms, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out a performer, a shop front or some planting.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the street up with the centre and keep your phone level, so the shop fronts lead the eye down the mall.
card.best_time: Try going early if you can, because it's a busy place and you may need to wait for a gap in the crowd. If the sun is low in front of you, tap the street and slide the picture a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against something steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Lincoln Road Mall sign with the pedestrian street behind you, so your selfie says exactly where you are. For something more dramatic, try the Colony Theater at the end of the street, which two blogs call the favourite photo spot. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more of the backdrop over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand beside the shallow pool that runs down the middle of the street, between 16th and 17th Streets, and ask a passer-by to frame you so the street's lines lead into the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a busy street, so watch your bag and phone when you stop to compose your shot. Lincoln Road Mall is public, but check the official site first if you plan to photograph inside a venue or at an event.
card.challenge: Grab a shot with a table or planter in the foreground and the whole mall stretching out behind it, with nobody walking through the middle. Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: Carl Fisher cleared the mangroves in 1912 to cut a strip across the island. In the 1950s the architect Morris Lapidus redesigned it in his Miami Modern ("MiMo") style, with gardens, fountains, shelters and an amphitheatre. It opened as a pedestrian mall on 28 November 1960 and joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Pennsylvania Avenue and stand about 210 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The whole length of the mall opens up in front of you.

card.hook: The Fontainebleau's big curved front is the shape everyone remembers, and it really shows off once the lights come on. Skip the flat daylight and save your battery for dusk.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement of Collins Avenue in Miami Beach and look north, so the curved front of the Fontainebleau sits to your right and leads your eye down the avenue.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the curved front down the avenue. Try zoom 0.5x for more street and sky, but keep the building away from the edges, where it can stretch. From further back, zoom 2x or more picks out the curve.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edge of the avenue so the building's vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go at dusk, when the building is lit and the sky still has some colour. Night works too, and after dark use night mode, tap the lit facade, and slide it a little darker so the lights don't wash out.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden boardwalk between the hotel and the beach, with palm trees in the frame. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and face the sea, so the hotel should end up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the Collins Avenue sidewalk in front of the curved facade and ask them to frame the hotel's curved front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Collins Avenue is a public street, but the hotel and its Ocean Lawn are private property where you may be asked to move on, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole curve running down the avenue in one shot, then take a few more, because passing traffic changes every picture.
card.good_to_know: Morris Lapidus designed the Fontainebleau, and it opened in 1954. It appears in the opening aerial shot after the credits of the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger. It joined the National Register of Historic Places in December 2008, the same year it reopened after a renovation of about $1 billion that added newer towers while keeping Lapidus's original look.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement of Collins Avenue in Miami Beach and look north, so the curved front of the Fontainebleau sits to your right and leads your eye down the avenue.

selfie_spots.why: A blogger's shoot used this boardwalk with palm trees for a tropical backdrop, and the Ocean Lawn is described as running along the beach and boardwalk, so the hotel should sit behind you when you face the sea.

None of the pages mention selfie sticks or tripods, and none give a safety point. The Collins Avenue spot is named by street and frontage, not a precise curb point.

card.hook: Imagine a whole street of pastel hotel fronts, curved corners and neon signs, all lined up like they're waiting for their picture. That's Ocean Drive, and it's very hard to take a bad photo here.
card.stand_here: Stand near Ocean Drive, about 510 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The line of Art Deco buildings leads your eye straight down the road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big street view. Switch to 0.5x when you want a whole hotel front, then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a sign or rooftop detail.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a pastel wall, then slide the brightness a little darker so the colours stay rich and the neon doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is quieter, and the light on the buildings is soft. Around dusk and after dark the neon comes on and the street looks completely different, so try both if you can.
card.selfie_here: Try the Ocean Drive sidewalk in front of the Beacon Hotel, with the neon-lit hotel front behind you. One photo guide calls it the most photographed spot on the street, and says it's best at night when the neon lights up. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it, to fit more of the building in.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the sand or beach path in Lummus Park and shoot back toward the park, while you stand with the Art Deco hotels behind you (sunrise or golden hour looks best).
card.rules_and_safety: After sunset, access, safety and light conditions change, so plan any night photos with that in mind. Ocean Drive is open to traffic again, so check the official site for current changes.
card.challenge: Find one neon sign, one curved corner and one café table, and see if you can get all three in a single shot.
card.good_to_know: Ocean Drive sits at the heart of the Miami Art Deco District, which has about 900 preserved buildings and is on the National Register of Historic Places. The street was developed in the 1920s and 1930s, and the rounded Streamline Moderne style dominates. The 1939 Colony Hotel is described as the most photographed Art Deco hotel here, and The Carlyle appeared in The Birdcage (1996).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Ocean Drive, about 510 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. The line of Art Deco buildings leads your eye straight down the road.

card.hook: Two hotels, one architect and a famously bitter rivalry: the Eden Roc is the formal, buttoned-up one, and it looks best once the sun goes down.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Mid-Beach stretch of Collins Avenue, right at the hotel, and face the tower. It's an area, not one exact spot, so shuffle along the pavement until no trees or signs are in the way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and step back until the whole tower fits. If the top gets chopped off, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x to pick out the finned sign structure on the roof (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go at night once the hotels are lit, when the glowing tower sits in a row with its Mid-Beach neighbours. Morning is better if you're shooting the beach side of the hotel.
card.selfie_here: For a sunset selfie, the hotel's pool deck at 4525 Collins Avenue is a good setup, though it's inside the hotel grounds, so access may depend on being a guest. Or try Indian Beach Park, the beach stretch between the Eden Roc and the Mimosa Condominium. Use the front camera, and try to get the hotel somewhere behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Collins Avenue is an ordinary public street, but the hotel's beachfront grounds may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the finned sign structure on the roofline, a palm tree and a streak of car lights all in one night shot.
card.good_to_know: Morris Lapidus designed the Eden Roc in the Miami Modern style, and it was finished in 1955–56. He built it just north of his own Fontainebleau, and the two hotels had a bitter rivalry. A 21-story Ocean Tower was added in 2008, and part of the building now operates as the Nobu Hotel Miami Beach.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Mid-Beach stretch of Collins Avenue, right at the hotel, and face the tower. It's an area, not one exact spot, so shuffle along the pavement until no trees or signs are in the way.

The only photo rule found is for the hotel's own photoshoot service, which <cite index="6-6">is bookable by reservation only</cite>; that is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so no rules are listed. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gives a safety point.

card.hook: Frank Gehry is famous for wild, curvy buildings, but the street side of this one is pale, calm and mostly rectangles. The curves are hiding inside. That makes it an easy one for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and 17th Street, on the corner facing the building's front. Face the New World Center and shoot across the SoundScape Park lawn.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the front of the building. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want the whole lawn and the building in one picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines so the building's upright edges line up with them and don't lean, and leave a band of lawn along the bottom of the frame.
card.best_time: Go after dark if you want the colourful video projections that can appear on the big wall, and check the programme for wallcast evenings. By day the plain front still photographs cleanly. Tap the pale wall and make the picture a touch darker so the white plaster keeps its detail. At night, switch on night mode and rest your elbows against a railing or your body to keep steady.
card.selfie_here: Head into SoundScape Park, right beside the building, and turn so the glass front fills the background. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit lower so the building sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the corner of Washington Avenue and 17th Street while you stand on the park side with the building behind you (check on site that the whole front fits).
card.rules_and_safety: The park is a public space, but events or closures can change what's on the lawn, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the lawn fills the bottom third and the building's edges sit perfectly straight on the grid. No leaning allowed.
card.good_to_know: The New World Center opened in January 2011 and is home to the New World Symphony. It seats 756 people. In front is a 2.5-acre public park, and the big wall shows free 'wallcasts' of concerts and video art. It is said to be the largest permanently installed projection surface in North America.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and 17th Street, on the corner facing the building's front. Face the New World Center and shoot across the SoundScape Park lawn.

card.hook: Ocean Drive is lined with plainer frontages, and then this old stone house with its ornate gates stops you mid-stride. It's the kind of front door that makes you reach for your phone before you've decided to.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public sidewalk in front of the Casa Casuarina gates, on the west side of Ocean Drive between 11th and 12th streets. Face west towards the house.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade and gates. If the sidewalk is busy and you can't step back, try 0.5x, and use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the stonework, the medallions or the rooftop observatory.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the gates and entrance in the centre, then tap the house and slide it a little darker if bright light washes out the stone.
card.best_time: Go when the gates are open, because closed gates hide most of the house. If people wander into your shot, wait a moment for a gap.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the front steps facing Ocean Drive, which two guides call the most photographed part of the house. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the facade fits, and keep the mansion over your shoulder, all from the public side of the gate.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the sidewalk across from the wrought iron gates and coral stone archway, and ask a passer-by to frame you with the gates and the steps behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The property doesn't allow photography on its grounds, so stay on the pavement and don't step through the gates. The steps are only for diners and overnight guests, so stay on the public side.
card.challenge: The walls carry about 100 medallions of historical figures, so zoom in and find the one with the best expression.
card.good_to_know: Casa Casuarina, also called the Versace Mansion, was built in 1930 for philanthropist Alden Freeman, who said it was modelled on the Alcázar de Colón. Gianni Versace lived here from 1992 until 1997. Since 2015 it has been a luxury hotel, The Villa Casa Casuarina.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public sidewalk in front of the Casa Casuarina gates, on the west side of Ocean Drive between 11th and 12th streets. Face west towards the house.

selfie_spots.name: Coquina steps out front on Ocean Drive, Casa Casuarina
selfie_spots.detail: on the front steps facing Ocean Drive, with the mansion's facade behind you
selfie_spots.why: Two guides call these steps the most photographed part of the house, and tourists pose there often; the steps are only for diners and overnight guests to climb past the gate, so stay on the public side.

card.hook: Joe's Stone Crab started out as a little seafood stand at a bathing casino, and now it's a Miami Beach landmark that deserves a proper street-level photo. You get to shoot the whole story from the pavement.
card.stand_here: From there the restaurant is about 78 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. Face north-east and keep the building, entrance and sign together in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole frontage. Drop to 0.5x only if the pavement is too narrow to step back, and keep the building centred so the edges don't stretch. For a closer shot of the sign or doorway, try 2x or more (depends on your phone) instead of stepping into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up a vertical edge of the building with a grid line so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light than midday. After dusk the lit sign makes a good night-mode photo, so rest your phone against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt it so the building sits behind your shoulder. Keep the sign in view and stay on the pavement.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside can be seen from the public street. It's a business though, so check the official site before you go inside or take photos in there.
card.challenge: Get the building, the entrance and the sign all in one shot, with a strip of pavement along the bottom to show where you are.
card.good_to_know: It all began in 1913, when Joe Weiss came to Miami Beach for his asthma and the family opened a seafood concession at Smith's Bathing Casino. Joe's Diner opened in 1920, and the restaurant became a Miami Beach historic landmark in 1975. It's still family-run, and fresh claws are served from 15 October to 1 May, the legal catch period.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map. From there the restaurant is about 78 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. Face north-east and keep the building, entrance and sign together in the frame.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with Joe's Stone Crab behind the photographer, or a standing point for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole building. Searches returned only menu photos, reviews, listings and interior shots. Tripadvisor has an 'exterior' photo (https://www.tripadvisor.com/LocationPhotoDirectLink-g34439-d465680-i445378048-Joe_s_Stone_Crab-Miami_Beach_Florida.html) but its text gives no position for the camera. Flickr (https://www.flickr.com/photos/wallyg/6664708439) confirms the restaurant is at 11 Washington Avenue, at the end of South Beach, but names no photo position. Yelp (https://www.yelp.com/biz/joes-stone-crab-miami-beach-3) lists an outdoor seating area and an outside photo count, not a viewpoint. No selfie-stick or tripod rules and no safety point were found on any page. Suggest a targeted search for Washington Avenue or Lincoln Road photo spots, or a local photo-guide page for the block, before adding any spot.

card.hook: The Delano is a tall white tower you can spot from the street, but the hedges out front love to play hide-and-seek with it. Walk the block until you find a gap and the whole thing pops into view.
card.stand_here: Stand on Collins Avenue, on the block in front of the Delano Miami Beach hotel. The hotel is to the east, so look along the strip with the towers rising above the pastel Art Deco hotels next door.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the hotel strip and the street, then switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the hotel. Try 2x (if your phone has it) to pick out the tower and the winged column.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright white walls, then drag the brightness down a touch so the building keeps its detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, when the sun is behind you as you look east at the hotel.
card.selfie_here: For something playful, try the Alice in Wonderland-themed garden path in the hotel grounds at 1685 Collins Ave. Forbes Travel Guide calls it a fun candid-photo spot, though it doesn't say the hotel shows up behind you. Use the front camera, and if you want more in the shot, try zoom 0.5x. That information is a few years old and the path may have changed since the renovation.
card.rules_and_safety: The Collins Avenue frontage is a public street, but the hotel is a private business. Check the official site for its current status and for any access to the hotel or grounds. Renovation work may also affect the view.
card.challenge: Line up the edge of the tower with a gridline so it stands perfectly straight, then see if you can fit the winged column in too.
card.good_to_know: The Delano opened on 15 December 1948 and was designed by B. Robert Swartburg. It has 14 storeys plus a 35-foot tower, and it's named after President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Philippe Starck led the 1994 renovation, and the hotel reopened in June 2026 after a redevelopment.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Collins Avenue, on the block in front of the Delano Miami Beach hotel. The hotel is to the east, so look along the strip with the towers rising above the pastel Art Deco hotels next door.

selfie_spots.name: Alice in Wonderland-themed garden path, Delano Miami Beach (1685 Collins Ave)
selfie_spots.detail: on the garden path inside the hotel grounds, which Forbes describes as Alice in Wonderland-themed
selfie_spots.why: Forbes Travel Guide calls this path a playful candid-shot spot, but the source does not say the hotel is framed behind the visitor.

sources.title: 8 Of Miami's Most Instagrammable Hotels (Forbes Travel Guide)

selfie_research.notes: Evidence is thin. Only one page (Forbes) names a photo spot at this hotel, and it is a candid garden-path shot, not a clear 'landmark behind you' selfie spot. The Forbes article is about 3,000 days old and may predate the 2025 renovation, so the garden path may have changed. I found no page naming a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole hotel, so ask_someone_spot is null. The hotel's own site says a path just beyond the pool opens onto the oceanfront Miami Beach Boardwalk, but no page calls that a photo spot, so I left it out. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules or a safety point.

card.hook: Picture a long green lawn, a row of palm trees and the Atlantic sparkling behind them, with pastel Art Deco buildings on the other side of the road. That's Lummus Park, and it looks good almost wherever you point your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at Ocean Drive at 6th Street, on the west side of Ocean Drive, and look across the road at the park and the ocean. The middle of the park is about 570 m (a short walk) to the north, along the park and the Promenade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the lawn, palms, ocean and Ocean Drive buildings all in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a palm tree and leave the crowds out.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on a lower line so the palms and lawn fill the bottom of the picture, and let the curvy Promenade lead the eye in.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, while weekends and midday get very busy. In the afternoon the sun should be behind you as you face the park and sea.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps of one of the lifeguard towers on the sand and face the ocean, so the park is behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit high to get the beach and palms over your shoulder; it works nicely at sunrise too.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to shoot from the sand on the beach side, aiming back toward the park so the green lawn and palms fill the frame, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for any events or temporary closures before you go. The colourful Miami Beach sign (between 5th and 6th Street) may be a temporary installation, so check it's still there.
card.challenge: Find the curve of the Promenade and take a shot where it sweeps toward a palm tree, with nobody walking in the frame.
card.good_to_know: Lummus Park covers about 74 acres (30 ha) and is named after the Lummus brothers, two of Miami's early pioneers. It was redesigned in the mid-1980s as part of the revival of the Art Deco district. You might spot it on screen too, as it has appeared in Miami Vice and Burn Notice.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Ocean Drive at 6th Street, on the west side of Ocean Drive, and look across the road at the park and the ocean. The middle of the park is about 570 m (a short walk) to the north, along the park and the Promenade.

selfie_spots.why: The elevated spot gives a bird's-eye view of the beach and works for sunrise selfies with the park behind.

card.hook: Picture a cruise ship the size of an apartment block sliding past while the Downtown Miami skyline sits right behind it. You get that show at the very tip of South Beach, and you don't need to do anything clever to catch it.
card.stand_here: Head for South Pointe Pier. From the southern end of South Beach, the middle of the park is about 400 m (roughly 5 minutes on foot) to the north-west. Walk out to the end of the pier and face across the channel toward the skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole pier and a big sky in the frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the sea and hotels. From the end of the pier, try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a ship or the skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the pier along one third of the frame and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Sunrise is the classic time here. Sunset and blue hour are lovely too, and kinder if you're not an early riser.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the grass near the Obstinate Lighthouse art piece at the park's southern end. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the lighthouse behind your shoulder. At the far end of the pier you can also take a selfie with Fisher Island as your backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The pier is generally open from around sunrise to sunset and can close in rough weather, so check the posted hours and the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a few frames as a ship passes, then pick the one where it sits neatly in front of the skyline, with no stray bins or strangers at the edges.
card.good_to_know: South Pointe Park is 17 acres and opened on 25 October 1985. It was redesigned by Hargreaves Associates, with the work finished around March 2009, which added the wide limestone-lined walkways. The pier is about 450 feet long, so it makes a natural line leading out over the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for South Pointe Pier. From the southern end of South Beach, the middle of the park is about 400 m (roughly 5 minutes on foot) to the north-west. Walk out to the end of the pier and face across the channel toward the skyline.

card.hook: Picture a museum built of warm, bumpy coral rock, with a palm tree on each side and a pond at your feet. That's the Bass, and it looks great from the grass.
card.stand_here: Stand in Collins Park, across the lawn from the main entrance. The museum is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so face north-west with the pond in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front with the palms and pond. If the lawn is busy and you can't step back, try zoom 0.5x, but keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't look stretched. Zoom 2x to 5x is good for the coral texture or the Eternity Now sculpture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the building's front on the upper or lower third line, and tap the coral-rock front, then drag the brightness slider a little darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light falls nicely on the coral rock.
card.selfie_here: Head to the five stacked, painted Miami Mountain boulders in Collins Park, the park's best-known photo spot. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the boulders fill the frame. Check on the spot that the museum shows up over your shoulder, because we couldn't confirm it sits right behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the park facing the main entrance, while you stand on the lawn in front of the museum so the whole facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside the galleries can differ from outdoors, so ask staff before you shoot inside. One travel blog says selfie sticks are usually not allowed in the galleries, though that's not an official policy.
card.challenge: Find the gap between the palms where no trunk cuts across the building, then take one shot with the pond in front and one with the boulders in front.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 1964 in a building that was once the Miami Beach Public Library. It was extended in 2002 with a wing by Arata Isozaki, and a further expansion by David Gauld reopened in 2017. Eternity Now (2015) by Sylvie Fleury and Miami Mountain (2016) by Ugo Rondinone were acquired together in 2016.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Collins Park, across the lawn from the main entrance. The museum is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so face north-west with the pond in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: It is the park's best-known photo-op, so visitors can pose in front of the stacked boulders with the museum close by, though no source confirms the museum is directly behind the selfie-taker.

card.hook: Española Way is narrow enough that café tables, painted walls and shop signs all squeeze into one frame, and your phone will love it. You can grab the wide scene and the close-up in the same few minutes.
card.stand_here: Stand near Española Way, about 680 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Then walk to one end of the street and shoot along it, with the buildings on both sides in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the street. Tap 0.5x when you want the whole narrow street in one go, and 2x (or more, depending on your phone) for signs and window details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a bright wall, then drag the slider to make it slightly darker so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, so you get cleaner views along the street. In the evening, switch on night mode for café lights and signs, and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head mid-block on Española Way, on the pink-walled stretch between Washington Avenue and Collins Avenue. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the pink facades and striped awnings behind you over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The street has cobblestones, so skip the heels to avoid twisted ankles. Individual cafés and venues set their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Build a three-layer shot: a café chair, lamp or doorway up front, then the street leading the eye to the far end. Wait a few seconds for walkers to clear.
card.good_to_know: Española Way is in South Beach, the part of Miami Beach south of Dade Boulevard. It was the first section of the city to be developed, from the 1910s onwards. In the 1930s the area filled with Art Deco, Streamline Moderne and Nautical Moderne buildings, and almost one square mile was protected as the Miami Beach Architectural District in 1979.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Española Way, about 680 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Then walk to one end of the street and shoot along it, with the buildings on both sides in the frame.

card.hook: Before you even reach the gate, you'll spot it: a huge bronze hand reaching up over the greenery. It's a quiet, powerful first look, and it's worth pausing for.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard, where the centre of the memorial is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. Face south-east and the hand rises above the trees in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from the street to fit the full height of the hand. Inside, try zoom 0.5x to get the tunnel and the figures into one frame, or zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to get close on the hand and fingers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and hold your phone upright, then tap the hand and drag the brightness down a touch so the bronze keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the bronze. Check the opening times on the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: This is a solemn place, so a selfie isn't really the point here. If you'd like a quiet record that you were here, the near edge of the reflecting pool, on the side you enter from, is where visitors tend to pause. Keep it simple and unposed, with the front camera and the arm behind you, and check the spot on site.
card.ask_someone: If you'd like a photo of yourself, ask someone to stand on the far side of the reflecting pool while you stand at the pool's near edge, so the sculpture and its reflection fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone use quiet and respectful, and avoid posed or playful pictures. Photography is generally allowed for personal use, but check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo with the hand filling the height of the frame and a little greenery at the bottom, then put your phone away and spend a quiet minute just looking.
card.good_to_know: A committee of survivors conceived the memorial in 1984, and Kenneth Treister designed it. It opened on 4 February 1990, with Elie Wiesel as guest speaker at the dedication. The site was once the family home of Holocaust survivors William and Florrie Loeb, and a few trees at the back were planted by the original owners in the 1920s and 1930s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Meridian Avenue and Dade Boulevard, where the centre of the memorial is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. Face south-east and the hand rises above the trees in front of you.

card.hook: Most museums make you step back and squint. This one sits right on a Miami Beach street corner, so you get the whole Mediterranean Revival facade and the everyday street life in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and 10th Street, in the Art Deco District. The Wolfsonian–FIU lies just to the north-east, so face that way and step back until the whole corner fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole corner facade in from the pavement. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the entrance and decoration.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so it doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Earlier or later in the day is likely to give you softer light and quieter pavements. Any time works for the outside, though.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Washington Avenue sidewalk in front of the carved stone entrance at 1001 Washington Ave, facing it with the building's front behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want more of the facade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Washington Avenue corner at 10th Street while you stand at the entrance, so they can get you with the full facade behind.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the exterior from the public street, but going inside is a museum visit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the facade with dead-straight vertical lines and not a single parked car in the way. Patience is the real skill here.
card.good_to_know: The building began as the Washington Storage Company facility, which had been operating since 1926. Collector Mitchell Wolfson Jr. stored his growing collection there, bought the building in 1986 and opened it as a museum in 1995. Inside are roughly 180,000 pieces dated 1885 to 1945, from furniture and glass to rare books.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and 10th Street, in the Art Deco District. The Wolfsonian–FIU lies just to the north-east, so face that way and step back until the whole corner fits.

card.hook: Picture a pastel hotel front, a blue neon sign and palm trees lined up like a postcard, with the beach just next door. The Colony Hotel does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk across the street from The Colony Hotel at 736 Ocean Drive and face the hotel. The middle of the district, as marked on the map, is about 955 m (roughly 12 minutes on foot) to the north of it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole hotel front. Switch to 0.5x if the pavement is crowded or you want more of the street. Try 2x or more for the neon sign and the Art Deco details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the hotel's centre up with the middle of the frame, because the front is symmetrical. Then tap the hotel and drag the brightness down a touch so the neon keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or sunset gives the nicest colour. Ocean Drive is busiest at night, so go earlier if you want fewer people in your shot. At dusk, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sidewalk in front of The Colony Hotel's entrance, where the vertical COLONY sign and the HOTEL lettering over the door are both in view. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the sign over your shoulder. Another good spot is the corner of 10th Street and Ocean Drive, with the pastel fronts running behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite side of Ocean Drive from the Park Central Hotel (640 Ocean Dr), while you stand in front of the building so its symmetrical front fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The Colony Hotel front and Lummus Park can be photographed from public pavement and parkland, but check the official site before you go for any access rules.
card.challenge: Get the hotel dead centre on the gridlines with the vertical lines perfectly straight, then take a second shot with a palm tree sneaking in.
card.good_to_know: The Miami Beach Architectural District has 960 historic buildings and was designated a historic district on 14 May 1979. It is described as the largest collection of Art Deco buildings in the world. Most were built between the Great Depression and the early 1940s, after the 1925 real estate slump and the 1926 hurricane.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sidewalk across the street from The Colony Hotel at 736 Ocean Drive and face the hotel. The middle of the district, as marked on the map, is about 955 m (roughly 12 minutes on foot) to the north of it.

card.hook: Ocean Drive is a row of Art Deco fronts all showing off, and The Tides is the one that stands head and shoulders above the rest. When it opened in 1936 it was the tallest building in Miami Beach, so it's used to being the star.
card.stand_here: Stand in Lummus Park, the green strip across Ocean Drive from the hotel on the beach side of the street. The hotel is to the west, so face west and look back over the palms at the Art Deco row, with The Tides among them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the palms and the whole Art Deco row in. Switch to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick The Tides out from its neighbours.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the tower upright, tap the hotel, then slide the picture a little darker so the sky and pale walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun may light the front of the building. Early is also best if you want fewer people on the street.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Ocean Drive pavement next to the decorative Art Deco lamp outside the hotel and put the facade behind you. Or face the recessed three-part entrance with its big porthole windows behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the building fits over your shoulder, and check on arrival that the spot works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Ocean Drive sidewalk outside 1220 Ocean Drive (between 12th and 13th Streets) to step back far enough to fit the whole building while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Lummus Park and Ocean Drive are public outdoor spaces, but the hotel is a private business. Check that it's operating before you plan a visit, and check the official site if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower is the tallest thing in the frame, and one where a palm tree tries to steal the show. Then pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: The Tides has 11 storeys and stands 49 metres tall. It was finished in 1936 and was one of the tallest buildings in Florida at the time. It was renovated in 1997 and is now a residential condominium and luxury hotel, currently known as the King & Grove Tides South Beach.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Lummus Park, the green strip across Ocean Drive from the hotel on the beach side of the street. The hotel is to the west, so face west and look back over the palms at the Art Deco row, with The Tides among them.

card.hook: While everyone else on the map is chasing the busy stuff, this church just sits there looking calm. That's its charm, so give it a proper portrait.
card.stand_here: Stand near Lincoln Road, about 70 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west towards Miami Beach Community Church.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the whole building and a bit of its street. If you want it bigger and fewer parked cars in the shot, try 2x if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with the vertical lines on screen, so the walls stand up straight.
card.best_time: Morning is a good bet, because the sun should be behind you as you face the church. Late afternoon can look lovely too, but you may be shooting towards the sun, so tap the church and make the picture a little darker if the sky is too bright.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold the phone a bit higher than your face. Try 0.5x if your phone has it, so you can fit the church over your shoulder as well as yourself. Step back until the whole building is in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship and may have set visiting times or rules, so check the official site before you go inside.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the whole church and its street, then one close-up of the entrance or a detail that catches your eye.
card.good_to_know: Miami Beach Community Church is a church building in Miami Beach, Florida. We don't have dates or history for it here, so the church's own website or noticeboard is the best place to learn more. Wait a moment and cars and people will pass, so you can get a clearer shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Lincoln Road, about 70 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west towards Miami Beach Community Church.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the church behind the visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole building. Most results were historic photos, Wikimedia file pages and a Yelp photo feed, with no photo-spot guidance. The one Lincoln Road photo guide I found points to the Lincoln Road Mall sign and the Colony Theater, not the church, so I left them out. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, and no page gives a safety point about this spot. Sources disagree on the building's current use: Wikimedia says the former church on Lincoln Road Mall has been repurposed as commercial space, while Yelp lists Miami Beach Community Church at 1620 Drexel Ave as an active congregation. Addresses also differ: the church is listed at 1620 Drexel Avenue, while the Lincoln Road Mall pages place the building on the mall, so check the street before sending anyone. The position you gave (25.79015, -80.13343) is roughly 170 m west of the church's mapped coordinates (25.790575, -80.134965) on Wikimedia Commons. A local photo-spot guide or a fresh search for Lincoln Road church photo spots would be needed to fill these fields.
